column3: Only your mother's brother: the father's brothers are 叔叔 and 伯伯. You call him 舅舅 to his face too, and his wife is 舅妈.
column6: Wǒ jiùjiu zhù zài Táizhōng.
column7: My uncle on my mother's side lives in Taichung.
column9: Only your mother's brother: the father's brothers are 叔叔 and 伯伯. You call him 舅舅 to his face too, and his wife is 舅媽.

column3: Used both to address her and to talk about her. She is the wife of 舅舅; your father's older brother's wife is 伯母 and his younger brother's wife is 婶婶.
column6: Jiùmā jīntiān zuò le hěn duō cài.
column7: My aunt cooked a lot of dishes today.
column9: Used both to address her and to talk about her. She is the wife of 舅舅; your father's older brother's wife is 伯母 and his younger brother's wife is 嬸嬸.

column3: The formal word for your father's father, for writing and introductions. In speech, and to his face, you say 爷爷. The mother's father is 外祖父 or 外公.
column6: Wǒ zǔfù jīnnián bāshí suì.
column7: My grandfather is eighty this year.
column9: The formal word for your father's father, for writing and introductions. In speech, and to his face, you say 爺爺. The mother's father is 外祖父 or 外公.

column3: The formal word for your father's mother, for writing and introductions; at home you say 奶奶. The mother's mother is 外祖母 or 外婆. 母 is a differentiated form of 女 with distinguishing dots added.
column6: Zǔmǔ xǐhuan zhòng huā.
column7: Grandmother likes to grow flowers.
column9: The formal word for your father's mother, for writing and introductions; at home you say 奶奶. The mother's mother is 外祖母 or 外婆. 母 is a differentiated form of 女 with distinguishing dots added.

column3: The formal word for your mother's father, seen in writing and on forms; in speech people say 外公. The 外 is put in front of 祖父 to mark the mother's side, and 外祖母 is her mother.
column6: Wǒ wàizǔfù shì lǎoshī.
column7: My maternal grandfather is a teacher.
column9: The formal word for your mother's father, seen in writing and on forms; in speech people say 外公. The 外 is put in front of 祖父 to mark the mother's side, and 外祖母 is her mother.

column3: The formal word for your mother's mother; in speech people say 外婆. Like 外祖父, it puts 外 in front to mark the mother's side, while the father's mother is 祖母.
column6: Wǒ wàizǔmǔ jīnnián qīshí suì.
column7: My maternal grandmother is seventy this year.
column9: The formal word for your mother's mother; in speech people say 外婆. Like 外祖父, it puts 外 in front to mark the mother's side, while the father's mother is 祖母.

column3: Ancestors as a whole, the people of a family or a nation who lived long ago, not one grandparent (that is 祖父 or 祖母). The usual verb is 拜: 拜祖先, a custom at New Year and at Qingming.
column4: 过年的时候我们要拜祖先。
column5: 過年的時候我們要拜祖先。
column6: Guònián de shíhou wǒmen yào bài zǔxiān.
column7: At New Year we pay respects to our ancestors.
column9: Ancestors as a whole, the people of a family or a nation who lived long ago, not one grandparent (that is 祖父 or 祖母). The usual verb is 拜: 拜祖先, a custom at New Year and at Qingming.

column3: Sisters as a group, older and younger together, so it counts 我有三个姊妹 without saying who is older. It also names linked things: 姊妹市 for sister cities, 姊妹校 for sister schools. Brothers and sisters together are 兄弟姊妹. Taiwan writes both 姊妹 and 姐妹; the mainland mostly writes 姐妹. Taiwan's dictionary reads 姊妹 zǐmèi, though 姊 alone is jiě.
column6: Wǒ yǒu sān ge zǐmèi.
column7: I have three sisters.
column9: Sisters as a group, older and younger together, so it counts 我有三個姊妹 without saying who is older. It also names linked things: 姊妹市 for sister cities, 姊妹校 for sister schools. Brothers and sisters together are 兄弟姊妹. Taiwan writes both 姊妹 and 姐妹; the mainland mostly writes 姐妹. Taiwan's dictionary reads 姊妹 zǐmèi, though 姊 alone is jiě.

column3: A fond word for a baby or small child, and just as often a doll: 洋娃娃 is a foreign-style doll and 布娃娃 a rag doll. 娃娃脸 is a round, youthful baby face.
column4: 她给女儿买了一个娃娃。
column5: 她給女兒買了一個娃娃。
column6: Tā gěi nǚ'ér mǎi le yī ge wáwa.
column7: She bought her daughter a doll.
column9: A fond word for a baby or small child, and just as often a doll: 洋娃娃 is a foreign-style doll and 布娃娃 a rag doll. 娃娃臉 is a round, youthful baby face.

column3: At school, a new student: 新生训练 is the orientation in Taiwan, while the mainland says 迎新 or 新生入学教育. A newborn is 新生儿, and in writing 新生 can also mean newly born or emerging: 新生事物.
column6: Xuéxiào huānyíng xīnshēng.
column7: The school welcomes the new students.
column9: At school, a new student: 新生訓練 is the orientation in Taiwan, while the mainland says 迎新 or 新生入學教育. A newborn is 新生兒, and in writing 新生 can also mean newly born or emerging: 新生事物.

column3: A romantic partner, with a poetic ring; in speech 男朋友 and 女朋友 are the everyday words, and 情人节 is Valentine's Day. In everyday mainland speech 情人 often means a partner in an affair, and a couple are 情侣; in Taiwan it is more often just a sweetheart.
column4: 情人节那天他送了她一束花。
column5: 情人節那天他送了她一束花。
column6: Qíngrén jié nà tiān tā sòng le tā yī shù huā.
column7: On Valentine's Day he gave her a bouquet.
column9: A romantic partner, with a poetic ring; in speech 男朋友 and 女朋友 are the everyday words, and 情人節 is Valentine's Day. In everyday mainland speech 情人 often means a partner in an affair, and a couple are 情侶; in Taiwan it is more often just a sweetheart.

column3: Said of the person whose love ended or who was left, and it takes no object: 我失恋了, never 失恋他. The act of splitting up is 分手; the 恋 here is the one in 恋爱 ‘romantic love’.
column6: Tā shīliàn le, xīnqíng bù hǎo.
column7: He has broken up with someone and is in a bad mood.
column9: Said of the person whose love ended or who was left, and it takes no object: 我失戀了, never 失戀他. The act of splitting up is 分手; the 戀 here is the one in 戀愛 ‘romantic love’.

column3: Being unattached: married or not matters less than having no partner. It comes after 是 or 还是: 我还是单身, and you can ask 你单身吗？ A single man is a 单身汉.
column6: Wǒ háishi dānshēn.
column7: I am still single.
column9: Being unattached: married or not matters less than having no partner. It comes after 是 or 還是: 我還是單身, and you can ask 你單身嗎？ A single man is a 單身漢.

column3: Marriage as a state or institution: 婚姻幸福, and 婚姻状况 on forms. It is a noun; the verb ‘to marry’ is 结婚. Since the Han dynasty people have speculated that 婚 is related to 昏 ‘dusk’, because weddings take place around dusk.
column6: Tāmen de hūnyīn hěn xìngfú.
column7: Their marriage is very happy.
column9: Marriage as a state or institution: 婚姻幸福, and 婚姻狀況 on forms. It is a noun; the verb ‘to marry’ is 結婚. Since the Han dynasty people have speculated that 婚 is related to 昏 ‘dusk’, because weddings take place around dusk.

column3: A criticism of someone, usually a man, who moves from one romantic partner to the next: 他很花心. It describes a character trait, so it takes 很 and no object. 花 can also mean lecherous in colloquial speech.
column6: Tīngshuō tā hěn huāxīn.
column7: I heard he is unfaithful.
column9: A criticism of someone, usually a man, who moves from one romantic partner to the next: 他很花心. It describes a character trait, so it takes 很 and no object. 花 can also mean lecherous in colloquial speech.

column3: To handle something with care so as not to waste or damage it: 爱惜时间, 爱惜东西, 爱惜身体, 爱惜名誉. It is not romantic love (that is 爱), but it can be used for people one values: 爱惜人才. In Taiwan the 惜 is read xí.
column6: Nǐ yào àixī shíjiān.
column7: You should make good use of your time.
column9: To handle something with care so as not to waste or damage it: 愛惜時間, 愛惜東西, 愛惜身體, 愛惜名譽. It is not romantic love (that is 愛), but it can be used for people one values: 愛惜人才. In Taiwan the 惜 is read xí.

column3: A written word for making friends: 交友网站, 交友要小心. In speech people say 交朋友. It often turns up on friend-finding and dating apps.
column6: Shàngwǎng jiāoyǒu yào xiǎoxīn.
column7: Be careful when making friends online.
column9: A written word for making friends: 交友網站, 交友要小心. In speech people say 交朋友. It often turns up on friend-finding and dating apps.

column3: Rarely used alone in speech; it lives in compounds for kinds of feeling: 感情, 爱情, 友情, 心情, and 事情 ‘matter’, where the feeling has faded. On its own it is something owed or remembered, as in 这份情.
column6: Zhè fèn qíng wǒ huì yǒngyuǎn jìzhù.
column7: I will always remember this kindness.
column9: Rarely used alone in speech; it lives in compounds for kinds of feeling: 感情, 愛情, 友情, 心情, and 事情 ‘matter’, where the feeling has faded. On its own it is something owed or remembered, as in 這份情.

column3: Said to congratulate someone on good news, followed by the person: 恭喜你. Doubled, 恭喜恭喜 is a warmer congratulation, common at New Year; the reply to 恭喜 is 谢谢 or 同喜. It fits weddings, a new baby, a promotion or the New Year, when 恭喜发财 is the set greeting.
column6: Gōngxǐ nǐ kǎoshàng dàxué!
column7: Congratulations on getting into university!
column9: Said to congratulate someone on good news, followed by the person: 恭喜你. Doubled, 恭喜恭喜 is a warmer congratulation, common at New Year; the reply to 恭喜 is 謝謝 or 同喜. It fits weddings, a new baby, a promotion or the New Year, when 恭喜發財 is the set greeting.

column3: A verb with its object built in, so 了 goes in the middle: 发了财. The wish 恭喜发财 is the standard New Year greeting, a hope for wealth.
column6: Xīnnián kuàilè, gōngxǐ fācái!
column7: Happy New Year, may you prosper!
column9: A verb with its object built in, so 了 goes in the middle: 發了財. The wish 恭喜發財 is the standard New Year greeting, a hope for wealth.

column3: Mostly found in wishes: 万事如意 and 称心如意 are blessings for the New Year, birthdays and weddings. Negated, 不如意 says that things are not going your way.
column6: Zhù nǐ wànshì rúyì.
column7: I wish you all the best.
column9: Mostly found in wishes: 萬事如意 and 稱心如意 are blessings for the New Year, birthdays and weddings. Negated, 不如意 says that things are not going your way.

column3: The verb is 放: 放鞭炮; fireworks are 烟火 in Taiwan and 烟花 on the mainland. Firecrackers go off at New Year, weddings and temple festivals, traditionally to scare away bad luck.
column4: 过年的时候大家放鞭炮。
column5: 過年的時候大家放鞭炮。
column6: Guònián de shíhou dàjiā fàng biānpào.
column7: At New Year everybody sets off firecrackers.
column9: The verb is 放: 放鞭炮; fireworks are 煙火 in Taiwan and 煙花 on the mainland. Firecrackers go off at New Year, weddings and temple festivals, traditionally to scare away bad luck.

column3: In Taiwan, "fireworks": 放烟火 "set off fireworks", 看烟火, and the New Year's Eve show at Taipei 101 is 跨年烟火. The mainland says 烟花. The older meaning is "smoke and fire" or "cooked food", as in 人间烟火. 烟 "smoke" has 火 on its left.
column4: 跨年的时候可以看烟火。
column5: 跨年的時候可以看煙火。
column6: Kuànián de shíhou kěyǐ kàn yānhuǒ.
column7: On New Year's Eve you can watch fireworks.
column9: In Taiwan, "fireworks": 放煙火 "set off fireworks", 看煙火, and the New Year's Eve show at Taipei 101 is 跨年煙火. The mainland says 煙花. The older meaning is "smoke and fire" or "cooked food", as in 人間煙火. 煙 "smoke" has 火 on its left.

column3: A reunion of family members who have been apart, as a verb that takes no object: 一家团圆. The 团圆饭 is the New Year's Eve dinner, and Mid-Autumn is the other holiday for it.
column4: 过年时，全家人都回来团圆。
column5: 過年時，全家人都回來團圓。
column6: Guònián shí, quánjiārén dōu huílái tuányuán.
column7: At New Year the whole family comes home for a reunion.
column9: A reunion of family members who have been apart, as a verb that takes no object: 一家團圓. The 團圓飯 is the New Year's Eve dinner, and Mid-Autumn is the other holiday for it.

column3: A host looking after guests with food, drink or a place to stay: 招待客人. As a noun it is the hospitality itself, which you thank for: 谢谢你的招待.
column6: Xièxie nǐmen de zhāodài.
column7: Thank you for your hospitality.
column9: A host looking after guests with food, drink or a place to stay: 招待客人. As a noun it is the hospitality itself, which you thank for: 謝謝你的招待.

column3: 玫瑰花 is the flower, counted with 朵 for one rose and 束 for a bunch; red roses are the gift for Valentine's Day.
column6: Tā sòng le tā yī duǒ méiguī.
column7: He gave her a rose.
column9: 玫瑰花 is the flower, counted with 朵 for one rose and 束 for a bunch; red roses are the gift for Valentine's Day.

column3: A four-character idiom for a life of pleasure, usually said with disapproval: 他只知道吃喝玩乐. It can also be light, about a vacation of nothing but fun.
column4: 他每天只知道吃喝玩乐。
column5: 他每天只知道吃喝玩樂。
column6: Tā měitiān zhǐ zhīdào chīhēwánlè.
column7: All he does every day is eat, drink and have fun.
column9: A four-character idiom for a life of pleasure, usually said with disapproval: 他只知道吃喝玩樂. It can also be light, about a vacation of nothing but fun.

column3: A short exclamation to catch someone's attention or to react to something unexpected or unwelcome: 哎，你的钥匙掉了！ 哎呀 is the stronger form. For a sigh, use 唉.
column6: Āi, nǐ de yàoshi diào le!
column7: Hey, you dropped your key!
column9: A short exclamation to catch someone's attention or to react to something unexpected or unwelcome: 哎，你的鑰匙掉了！ 哎呀 is the stronger form. For a sigh, use 唉.

column3: A sigh of disappointment or sadness: 唉，今天又下雨了. Answering ‘yes’ when someone calls you (小明！) is mostly written 哎 instead, which is a sudden reaction or a call for attention.
column6: Āi, jīntiān yòu xiàyǔ le.
column7: Sigh, it's raining again today.
column9: A sigh of disappointment or sadness: 唉，今天又下雨了. Answering ‘yes’ when someone calls you (小明！) is mostly written 哎 instead, which is a sudden reaction or a call for attention.

column3: A casual ‘hi’ between friends and young people, borrowed from English; it is lighter than 你好 and out of place in a formal meeting. In slang it also means ‘high’, thrilled: 今晚玩得很嗨.
column6: Hāi, hǎojiǔ bù jiàn!
column7: Hi, long time no see!
column9: A casual ‘hi’ between friends and young people, borrowed from English; it is lighter than 你好 and out of place in a formal meeting. In slang it also means ‘high’, thrilled: 今晚玩得很嗨.

column3: Two uses in Taiwan. As an interjection: "oh, I see", when you understand something: 喔，我知道了. And at the end of a sentence it softens the tone, as a gentle reminder: 小心喔 "be careful, okay", 好喔 "okay". The second use is very typical of Taiwan speech. It is also written 哦.
column6: Ō, wǒ zhīdào le.
column7: Oh, I see.
column9: Two uses in Taiwan. As an interjection: "oh, I see", when you understand something: 喔，我知道了. And at the end of a sentence it softens the tone, as a gentle reminder: 小心喔 "be careful, okay", 好喔 "okay". The second use is very typical of Taiwan speech. It is also written 哦.

column3: A short reaction. Said with a rising pitch it shows doubt or surprise: 哦？真的吗？ With a falling pitch it means ‘oh, I see’, once you have just understood something. The mainland writes both as 哦, while in Taiwan the second is often written 喔.
column6: Ó? Zhēn de ma?
column7: Oh? Really?
column9: A short reaction. Said with a rising pitch it shows doubt or surprise: 哦？真的嗎？ With a falling pitch it means ‘oh, I see’, once you have just understood something. The mainland writes both as 哦, while in Taiwan the second is often written 喔.

column3: A sentence-final particle that says ‘this is obvious’, sometimes with a little impatience or a wish to persuade: 这是你自己说的嘛, 好嘛 ‘come on, okay’. It can also mark a pause after the topic: 你嘛，就别去了.
column6: Zhè shì nǐ zìjǐ shuō de ma.
column7: But you said it yourself.
column9: A sentence-final particle that says ‘this is obvious’, sometimes with a little impatience or a wish to persuade: 這是你自己說的嘛, 好嘛 ‘come on, okay’. It can also mark a pause after the topic: 你嘛，就別去了.

column3: A hum showing that you are listening or agree, like ‘mm-hm’: 嗯，我同意. Said with a rising pitch it asks ‘huh?’, and with a falling pitch it is a doubtful ‘hmm’ or a quiet yes.
column6: En, wǒ tóngyì.
column7: Mm, I agree.
column9: A hum showing that you are listening or agree, like ‘mm-hm’: 嗯，我同意. Said with a rising pitch it asks ‘huh?’, and with a falling pitch it is a doubtful ‘hmm’ or a quiet yes.

column3: Two uses. As an answer it means ‘that’s right!’: 对了！就是这样. At the start of a sentence, followed by a new topic, it means ‘oh, by the way’, for something you just remembered.
column6: Duìle, nǐ míngtiān yǒu kòng ma?
column7: Oh, by the way, are you free tomorrow?
column9: Two uses. As an answer it means ‘that’s right!’: 對了！就是這樣. At the start of a sentence, followed by a new topic, it means ‘oh, by the way’, for something you just remembered.

column3: Said to drop a subject, give up on something or tell someone not to worry: 算了，不要吵了. It can sound resigned or a little annoyed. Literally the matter is counted as finished.
column6: Suànle, wǒmen xiàcì zài qù.
column7: Forget it, we'll go next time.
column9: Said to drop a subject, give up on something or tell someone not to worry: 算了，不要吵了. It can sound resigned or a little annoyed. Literally the matter is counted as finished.

column3: Said after you learn the reason, to show that the result is no surprise: 难怪你这么累. It is followed by the result, often with 这么. 怪不得 means the same.
column6: Nánguài nǐ zhème lèi.
column7: No wonder you are so tired.
column9: Said after you learn the reason, to show that the result is no surprise: 難怪你這麼累. It is followed by the result, often with 這麼. 怪不得 means the same.

column3: It marks something obvious, at the start of a sentence: 不用说，他一定会来. It can also mean ‘no need to speak’, as in 你不用说了, so the next words decide which one it is.
column6: Bùyòngshuō, tā yīdìng huì lái.
column7: Needless to say, he will come.
column9: It marks something obvious, at the start of a sentence: 不用說，他一定會來. It can also mean ‘no need to speak’, as in 你不用說了, so the next words decide which one it is.

column3: Thin noodles of rice, in dishes such as 炒米粉 and 米粉汤; wheat noodles are 面条. It can also mean rice flour.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng chī chǎo mǐfěn.
column7: I'd like to eat fried rice noodles.
column9: Thin noodles of rice, in dishes such as 炒米粉 and 米粉湯; wheat noodles are 麵條. It can also mean rice flour.

column3: Wheat noodles of any kind, as against 米粉; in speech often just 面: 吃面, 牛肉面. Here 条 means a strip, as in 薯条, and it is also the measure word for long thin things.
column6: Wǒ wǔfàn xiǎng chī miàntiáo.
column7: I'd like to eat noodles for lunch.
column9: Wheat noodles of any kind, as against 米粉; in speech often just 麵: 吃麵, 牛肉麵. Here 條 means a strip, as in 薯條, and it is also the measure word for long thin things.

column3: Boiled dumplings, as against pan-fried 锅贴; In Taiwan 水饺 is the everyday word for dumplings, while the mainland mostly says 饺子. They are counted with 个: 十个水饺, and made with the verb 包: 包水饺. One scholar says 饺 comes from 角 ‘horn’, named for the dumpling's horn-like shape.
column6: Wǒmen bāo shuǐjiǎo ba.
column7: Let's make dumplings.
column9: Boiled dumplings, as against pan-fried 鍋貼; In Taiwan 水餃 is the everyday word for dumplings, while the mainland mostly says 餃子. They are counted with 個: 十個水餃, and made with the verb 包: 包水餃. One scholar says 餃 comes from 角 ‘horn’, named for the dumpling's horn-like shape.

column3: The vinegar you dip in: 沾醋 in Taiwan, 蘸醋 on the mainland. 吃醋, ‘to eat vinegar’, also means to be jealous, above all in love: 她看到他和别人聊天就吃醋了.
column4: 我喜欢在面里加一点醋。
column5: 我喜歡在麵裡加一點醋。
column6: Wǒ xǐhuan zài miàn lǐ jiā yīdiǎn cù.
column7: I like to add a little vinegar to my noodles.
column9: The vinegar you dip in: 沾醋 in Taiwan, 蘸醋 on the mainland. 吃醋, ‘to eat vinegar’, also means to be jealous, above all in love: 她看到他和別人聊天就吃醋了.

column3: The everyday soy sauce for the table, though it has no oil in it. On the mainland 生抽 is the light kind and 老抽 the darker one; in Taiwan 酱油膏 is a thicker, sweeter kind for dipping.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yīdiǎn jiàngyóu.
column7: Please give me a little soy sauce.
column9: The everyday soy sauce for the table, though it has no oil in it. On the mainland 生抽 is the light kind and 老抽 the darker one; in Taiwan 醬油膏 is a thicker, sweeter kind for dipping.

column3: Your taste in flavors: 口味重 likes strong flavors, 口味清淡 likes light food, 合我的口味 suits my taste. It is also the ‘flavor’ of a product, as on drinks and chips: 什么口味？
column6: Zhè dào cài hěn hé wǒ de kǒuwèi.
column7: This dish suits my taste.
column9: Your taste in flavors: 口味重 likes strong flavors, 口味清淡 likes light food, 合我的口味 suits my taste. It is also the ‘flavor’ of a product, as on drinks and chips: 什么口味？

column3: To cook in liquid, usually by boiling: 煮面, 煮水, 煮咖啡. In Taiwan 煮饭 is cooking a meal in general; in northern mainland speech it is cooking rice, and 做饭 is the general word. 炒 is stir-frying and 烤 is baking, so 煮 is the water-and-heat one.
column6: Wǒ lái zhǔ fàn, nǐ qù mǎi cài.
column7: I'll cook, you go and buy groceries.
column9: To cook in liquid, usually by boiling: 煮麵, 煮水, 煮咖啡. In Taiwan 煮飯 is cooking a meal in general; in northern mainland speech it is cooking rice, and 做飯 is the general word. 炒 is stir-frying and 烤 is baking, so 煮 is the water-and-heat one.

column3: A professional cook in a restaurant or hotel; someone who cooks at home just 做饭 and is not called a 厨师. The 师 ends many names of skilled trades: 老师, 医师, 律师, 设计师.
column4: 这家餐厅的厨师很有名。
column5: 這家餐廳的廚師很有名。
column6: Zhè jiā cāntīng de chúshī hěn yǒumíng.
column7: The chef of this restaurant is famous.
column9: A professional cook in a restaurant or hotel; someone who cooks at home just 做飯 and is not called a 廚師. The 師 ends many names of skilled trades: 老師, 醫師, 律師, 設計師.

column3: The azuki bean, sweetened for desserts: 红豆汤, 红豆饼, 红豆面包. Cooked with sugar until soft, it becomes a paste for fillings, a dessert soup, or a topping on shaved ice.
column6: Zhège miànbāo lǐ yǒu hóngdòu.
column7: This bread has red bean inside.
column9: The azuki bean, sweetened for desserts: 紅豆湯, 紅豆餅, 紅豆麵包. Cooked with sugar until soft, it becomes a paste for fillings, a dessert soup, or a topping on shaved ice.

column3: Plain hot water is a common drink, and 多喝热水 is the stock advice to someone who feels unwell. Other words: 热水器 for a water heater, 洗热水澡 for a hot bath.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī bēi rèshuǐ.
column7: Please give me a cup of hot water.
column9: Plain hot water is a common drink, and 多喝熱水 is the stock advice to someone who feels unwell. Other words: 熱水器 for a water heater, 洗熱水澡 for a hot bath.

column3: A polite phrase for the server or host to say when food is set down: 请慢用, and the guest answers 谢谢. It also fits tea and snacks. Literally ‘take your time with it’.
column6: Cài lái le, qǐng mànyòng.
column7: Here is your food, please enjoy.
column9: A polite phrase for the server or host to say when food is set down: 請慢用, and the guest answers 謝謝. It also fits tea and snacks. Literally ‘take your time with it’.

column3: To burst or blow up: 炸弹 for a bomb, 爆炸 for an explosion, 气球炸了. Informally it also means to flare up in anger.
column6: Qìqiú zhà le.
column7: The balloon burst.
column9: To burst or blow up: 炸彈 for a bomb, 爆炸 for an explosion, 氣球炸了. Informally it also means to flare up in anger.

column3: A leather belt for pants; you put it on with 系: 系皮带, and count it with 条: 一条皮带. The 带 is also the verb ‘to carry’: 带钱. 带 began as a picture of a woven belt.
column6: Tā de pídài shì hēisè de.
column7: His belt is black.
column9: A leather belt for pants; you put it on with 繫: 繫皮帶, and count it with 條: 一條皮帶. The 帶 is also the verb ‘to carry’: 帶錢. 帶 began as a picture of a woven belt.

column3: Makeup products in general; 化妆 is the verb ‘to put on makeup’. 品 ends many product words: 食品 for food products, 用品 for supplies, 药品 for medicine. 品 is three 口, representing various objects.
column6: Tā mǎi le hěn duō huàzhuāngpǐn.
column7: She bought a lot of cosmetics.
column9: Makeup products in general; 化妝 is the verb ‘to put on makeup’. 品 ends many product words: 食品 for food products, 用品 for supplies, 藥品 for medicine. 品 is three 口, representing various objects.

column3: You put it on by spraying, so the verb is 喷: 喷香水. The bottle is counted with 瓶, and the scent itself is just 香 (这瓶香水很香).
column6: Zhè píng xiāngshuǐ hěn xiāng.
column7: This perfume smells nice.
column9: You put it on by spraying, so the verb is 噴: 噴香水. The bottle is counted with 瓶, and the scent itself is just 香 (這瓶香水很香).

column3: Counted with 个, and clothes are stored "in" it: 衣服在衣柜里. A near-synonym is 衣橱, also a clothes cupboard.
column6: Yīfu dōu zài yīguì lǐ.
column7: All the clothes are in the wardrobe.
column9: Counted with 個, and clothes are stored "in" it: 衣服在衣櫃裡. A near-synonym is 衣櫥, also a clothes cupboard.

column3: It goes before a verb and says the effort or the thing spent got no result: 白白浪费, 白白等了很久. It can also be the plain color word, as in 白白的.
column6: Wǒ báibái děng le liǎng ge xiǎoshí.
column7: I waited two hours for nothing.
column9: It goes before a verb and says the effort or the thing spent got no result: 白白浪費, 白白等了很久. It can also be the plain color word, as in 白白的.

column3: Said of a man with good looks and an air of spirit: 英俊的男生. The casual word is 帅 (很帅); for women, 漂亮 or 美 is used instead.
column6: Tā yòu gāo yòu yīngjùn.
column7: He is tall and handsome.
column9: Said of a man with good looks and an air of spirit: 英俊的男生. The casual word is 帥 (很帥); for women, 漂亮 or 美 is used instead.

column3: The everyday word for the shoulder; 肩 alone turns up mostly in compounds. It goes with 宽 (broad), 酸 (sore) and the action 拍肩膀, patting someone on the shoulder.
column6: Tā de jiānbǎng hěn kuān.
column7: His shoulders are broad.
column9: The everyday word for the shoulder; 肩 alone turns up mostly in compounds. It goes with 寬 (broad), 酸 (sore) and the action 拍肩膀, patting someone on the shoulder.

column3: The full word, used for teeth in general; in speech 牙 alone is just as common, as in 刷牙 and 牙医. 牙 began as a picture of a pair of elephant tusks.
column6: Tā de yáchǐ hěn bái.
column7: His teeth are very white.
column9: The full word, used for teeth in general; in speech 牙 alone is just as common, as in 刷牙 and 牙醫. 牙 began as a picture of a pair of elephant tusks.

column3: It goes with 流 and 出 for bleeding (流血, 出血), and with 验 for a blood test (验血). It is a drop of blood inside a chalice, used for sacrifices.
column6: Wǒ bù gǎn kàn xiě.
column7: I don't dare look at blood.
column9: It goes with 流 and 出 for bleeding (流血, 出血), and with 驗 for a blood test (驗血). It is a drop of blood inside a chalice, used for sacrifices.

column3: Mostly met in compounds: 电脑 (computer), 大脑 (the brain), 头脑 (mind) and the spoken 脑子. 动脑 means to use your head.
column6: Tā de nǎo zi hěn cōngmíng.
column7: His mind is very sharp.
column9: Mostly met in compounds: 電腦 (computer), 大腦 (the brain), 頭腦 (mind) and the spoken 腦子. 動腦 means to use your head.

column3: A verb with its object, so it splits: 流了很多血, 流血了. It is also used for violence in general, as in 流血冲突.
column6: Nǐ de shǒuzhǐ zài liúxuè.
column7: Your finger is bleeding.
column9: A verb with its object, so it splits: 流了很多血, 流血了. It is also used for violence in general, as in 流血衝突.

column3: The everyday, not rude way to say it, and what a doctor will ask: 你拉肚子多久了? A verb with its object, so it splits: 拉了三次肚子. 腹泻 is the written, medical word.
column4: 我吃坏了东西，一直拉肚子。
column5: 我吃壞了東西，一直拉肚子。
column6: Wǒ chī huài le dōngxi, yīzhí lādùzi.
column7: I ate something bad and keep having diarrhea.
column9: The everyday, not rude way to say it, and what a doctor will ask: 你拉肚子多久了? A verb with its object, so it splits: 拉了三次肚子. 腹瀉 is the written, medical word.

column3: Illegal drugs, not medicine (that is 药). It appears in 毒品案 (a drug case) and 毒贩 (a dealer). 品 marks kinds of goods, as in 食品 and 商品. 品 is three 口 piled up, standing for various objects.
column6: Dúpǐn duì shēntǐ hěn bù hǎo.
column7: Drugs are very bad for the body.
column9: Illegal drugs, not medicine (that is 藥). It appears in 毒品案 (a drug case) and 毒販 (a dealer). 品 marks kinds of goods, as in 食品 and 商品. 品 is three 口 piled up, standing for various objects.

column3: The usual verb for taking illegal drugs, with the user called 吸毒者 and quitting called 戒毒. 吸 has 及 in it, which originally comes from "grab", so the idea is grabbing air through the mouth.
column6: Xīdú shì fànfǎ de.
column7: Taking drugs is against the law.
column9: The usual verb for taking illegal drugs, with the user called 吸毒者 and quitting called 戒毒. 吸 has 及 in it, which originally comes from "grab", so the idea is grabbing air through the mouth.

column3: You "have" one with 发生 or the everyday 出: 发生车祸, 出车祸. It covers a crash of any road vehicle, not only a car.
column6: Zuótiān lùshang fāshēng le chēhuò.
column7: There was a traffic accident on the road yesterday.
column9: You "have" one with 發生 or the everyday 出: 發生車禍, 出車禍. It covers a crash of any road vehicle, not only a car.

column3: Counted with 条: 一条命. It turns up in 生命, 命运 and 命令, and 救命! is the shout for help.
column6: Yīshēng jiù le tā de mìng.
column7: The doctor saved his life.
column9: Counted with 條: 一條命. It turns up in 生命, 命運 and 命令, and 救命! is the shout for help.

column3: It names the moment of waking up, so it goes with a time: 六点就醒来了. It is not 起床, which is getting out of bed. 醒 alone also works, as in 醒了.
column6: Wǒ jīntiān liù diǎn jiù xǐnglái le.
column7: I woke up at six today.
column9: It names the moment of waking up, so it goes with a time: 六點就醒來了. It is not 起床, which is getting out of bed. 醒 alone also works, as in 醒了.

column3: A written, formal syllable found in compounds: 着装 (attire), 穿着 (clothing), 着手 (set about), 着陆 (land, of a plane). Everyday speech uses 穿 for to wear.
column6: Tā shēn zhuó hēisè xīzhuāng chūxí.
column7: He attended wearing a black suit.
column9: A written, formal syllable found in compounds: 著裝 (attire), 穿著 (clothing), 著手 (set about), 著陸 (land, of a plane). Everyday speech uses 穿 for to wear.

column3: A verb with its object, so it splits: 作了一个梦. It also means wishful thinking: 别作梦了! Also written 做梦, the usual form on the mainland.
column6: Bié zuòmèng le!
column7: Stop dreaming!
column9: A verb with its object, so it splits: 作了一個夢. It also means wishful thinking: 別作夢了! Also written 做夢, the usual form on the mainland.

column3: Two uses. As "morning and evening" it names times of day: 早晚各一次. As "sooner or later" it goes before the verb, often with 会 or 都; 迟早 means the same.
column6: Tā zǎowǎn huì míngbai de.
column7: He will understand sooner or later.
column9: Two uses. As "morning and evening" it names times of day: 早晚各一次. As "sooner or later" it goes before the verb, often with 會 or 都; 遲早 means the same.

column3: Said of everyday life with its ups and downs, often of a couple or family: 好好过日子, 穷日子也要过. It can suggest living carefully with money.
column6: Wǒmen yīqǐ hǎohǎo guòrìzi.
column7: Let's live our lives well together.
column9: Said of everyday life with its ups and downs, often of a couple or family: 好好過日子, 窮日子也要過. It can suggest living carefully with money.

column3: An apartment building. In Taiwan 公寓 usually means an older, low building of four or five floors without an elevator, as against 大楼 for a tall modern one with an elevator. A single apartment is 一户. 寓 has 宀 "roof" for the meaning and 禺 for the sound (yù).
column4: 我住在一栋公寓的三楼。
column5: 我住在一棟公寓的三樓。
column6: Wǒ zhù zài yī dòng gōngyù de sān lóu.
column7: I live on the third floor of an apartment building.
column9: An apartment building. In Taiwan 公寓 usually means an older, low building of four or five floors without an elevator, as against 大樓 for a tall modern one with an elevator. A single apartment is 一戶. 寓 has 宀 "roof" for the meaning and 禺 for the sound (yù).

column3: The person renting a room or apartment. The landlord is 房东 and the rent is 房租.
column6: Zhè jiān fángzi yǒu sān ge fángkè.
column7: This house has three tenants.
column9: The person renting a room or apartment. The landlord is 房東 and the rent is 房租.

column3: The floor you walk on, whether wood, tile or carpet: 拖地板 (mop it), 扫地板 (sweep it). For a floor of a building, as in the second floor, say 楼 instead.
column6: Dìbǎn hěn gānjìng.
column7: The floor is very clean.
column9: The floor you walk on, whether wood, tile or carpet: 拖地板 (mop it), 掃地板 (sweep it). For a floor of a building, as in the second floor, say 樓 instead.

column3: The toilet bowl itself, not the room: 冲马桶 (flush it), 马桶盖 (the lid), 马桶堵了 (it is clogged). For the room, say 厕所 or 洗手间.
column6: Mǎtǒng huài le, qǐng zhǎo rén lái xiū.
column7: The toilet is broken, please get someone to fix it.
column9: The toilet bowl itself, not the room: 沖馬桶 (flush it), 馬桶蓋 (the lid), 馬桶堵了 (it is clogged). For the room, say 廁所 or 洗手間.

column3: A written-style word that usually follows its noun in four-character phrases: 乐趣无穷, 后患无穷. Before a noun it takes 的: 无穷的力量.
column6: Zhège yóuxì de lèqù wúqióng.
column7: The fun of this game is endless.
column9: A written-style word that usually follows its noun in four-character phrases: 樂趣無窮, 後患無窮. Before a noun it takes 的: 無窮的力量.

column3: The spoken, slightly longer form of 这样. It goes before a verb or stands alone in an answer: 这样子做不行, 原来是这样子.
column6: Nǐ bùyào zhèyàngzi shuōhuà.
column7: Don't talk like that.
column9: The spoken, slightly longer form of 這樣. It goes before a verb or stands alone in an answer: 這樣子做不行, 原來是這樣子.

column3: It goes before the verb and says something nearly happened but did not: 我差点迟到, 差点忘了. With a bad outcome, 差点没 means the same: 差点没摔倒 is also "nearly fell".
column4: 我差点忘了今天有考试。
column5: 我差點忘了今天有考試。
column6: Wǒ chàdiǎn wàng le jīntiān yǒu kǎoshì.
column7: I almost forgot that there is an exam today.
column9: It goes before the verb and says something nearly happened but did not: 我差點遲到, 差點忘了. With a bad outcome, 差點沒 means the same: 差點沒摔倒 is also "nearly fell".

column3: Properly, well, carefully, used before a verb to urge someone to do it thoroughly: 好好休息 "get a good rest", 好好学 "study hard". The dictionary's form with 儿 is northern; in Taiwan people say 好好 and usually write 好好的 or 好好地. The second 好 is read in the first tone when the 儿 is added.
column6: Nǐ yào hǎohāor xiūxi.
column7: You must get a good rest.
column9: Properly, well, carefully, used before a verb to urge someone to do it thoroughly: 好好休息 "get a good rest", 好好學 "study hard". The dictionary's form with 兒 is northern; in Taiwan people say 好好 and usually write 好好的 or 好好地. The second 好 is read in the first tone when the 兒 is added.

column3: In Taiwan 虫 alone is an everyday word; on the mainland the spoken word is usually 虫子. Figuratively a person with a habit can be one: 书虫 is a bookworm.
column6: Huāyuán lǐ yǒu hěn duō chóng.
column7: There are many bugs in the garden.
column9: In Taiwan 蟲 alone is an everyday word; on the mainland the spoken word is usually 蟲子. Figuratively a person with a habit can be one: 書蟲 is a bookworm.

column3: Counted with 只: 一只蚂蚁. 蚂蚁搬家 (ants moving house) is a saying taken as a sign that rain is coming.
column6: Zhuōshang yǒu hěn duō mǎyǐ.
column7: There are a lot of ants on the table.
column9: Counted with 隻: 一隻螞蟻. 螞蟻搬家 (ants moving house) is a saying taken as a sign that rain is coming.

column3: Found only in compounds: 狮子 for "a lion", 雄狮 (a male lion), 海狮 (a sea lion) and 狮子座 (Leo).
column6: Dòngwùyuán lǐ yǒu yī zhī shī zi.
column7: There is a lion at the zoo.
column9: Found only in compounds: 獅子 for "a lion", 雄獅 (a male lion), 海獅 (a sea lion) and 獅子座 (Leo).

column3: Counted with 只: 一只狮子. 狮子座 is the zodiac sign Leo, and 石狮 are the pair of stone lions at a temple gate. The word for lion is possibly of Iranian origin.
column6: Dòngwùyuán lǐ yǒu liǎng zhī shīzi.
column7: There are two lions in the zoo.
column9: Counted with 隻: 一隻獅子. 獅子座 is the zodiac sign Leo, and 石獅 are the pair of stone lions at a temple gate. The word for lion is possibly of Iranian origin.

column3: The spoken word, counted with 只: 一只兔子. 兔年 is the year of the rabbit, 小白兔 the "little white rabbit" of children's songs, and the moon rabbit is 玉兔.
column6: Tùzi xǐhuan chī cǎo.
column7: Rabbits like to eat grass.
column9: The spoken word, counted with 只: 一只兔子. 兔年 is the year of the rabbit, 小白兔 the "little white rabbit" of children's songs, and the moon rabbit is 玉兔.

column3: Mostly in compounds: 鸭子 (the spoken word), 烤鸭 (roast duck), 鸭肉 and 鸭蛋. The measure word is 只. The name is probably onomatopoeic in origin.
column6: Wǒmen diǎn le yī zhī kǎo yā.
column7: We ordered a roast duck.
column9: Mostly in compounds: 鴨子 (the spoken word), 烤鴨 (roast duck), 鴨肉 and 鴨蛋. The measure word is 隻. The name is probably onomatopoeic in origin.

column3: 老 is only a prefix here, as in 老鼠, with nothing to do with age. Counted with 只: 一只老虎. 纸老虎 (paper tiger) is someone who only looks fierce.
column6: Lǎohǔ bǐ māo dà hěn duō.
column7: A tiger is much bigger than a cat.
column9: 老 is only a prefix here, as in 老鼠, with nothing to do with age. Counted with 隻: 一隻老虎. 紙老虎 (paper tiger) is someone who only looks fierce.

column3: Giant panda, literally "bear cat". Today most people in Taiwan say 熊猫; older people may say 猫熊 "cat bear". 熊 is "bear"; 猫 "cat" has 犭 for the animal and 苗 for the sound (miáo, close to māo). The Taipei Zoo is known for its pandas.
column6: Táiběi dòngwùyuán yǒu xióngmāo.
column7: The Taipei Zoo has pandas.
column9: Giant panda, literally "bear cat". Today most people in Taiwan say 熊貓; older people may say 貓熊 "cat bear". 熊 is "bear"; 貓 "cat" has 豸 for the animal and 苗 for the sound (miáo, close to māo). The Taipei Zoo is known for its pandas.

column3: Trees as a group, with the feel of written Chinese: 保护树木, 树木茂盛. A single tree is 树 with the measure word 棵: 一棵树; 树木 is not counted that way.
column6: Gōngyuán lǐ yǒu hěn duō shùmù.
column7: There are many trees in the park.
column9: Trees as a group, with the feel of written Chinese: 保護樹木, 樹木茂盛. A single tree is 樹 with the measure word 棵: 一棵樹; 樹木 is not counted that way.

column3: A named or large island takes the measure word 座: 那座岛. It is part of many names: 小岛, 岛屿, 半岛 (peninsula) and 离岛 (an outlying island).
column6: Wǒmen zuò chuán qù nà zuò dǎo.
column7: We take a boat to that island.
column9: A named or large island takes the measure word 座: 那座島. It is part of many names: 小島, 島嶼, 半島 (peninsula) and 離島 (an outlying island).

column3: The ocean as a whole, in a general or scientific sense: 海洋生物, 海洋污染, 保护海洋. For going to the sea, people say 海 or 海边, not 海洋. 洋 also came to mean "foreign", because Western countries lay across the 西洋 and Europeans often arrived by ship.
column6: Hǎiyáng lǐ yǒu hěn duō yú.
column7: There are many fish in the ocean.
column9: The ocean as a whole, in a general or scientific sense: 海洋生物, 海洋污染, 保護海洋. For going to the sea, people say 海 or 海邊, not 海洋. 洋 also came to mean "foreign", because Western countries lay across the 西洋 and Europeans often arrived by ship.

column3: You go there to play or sun yourself: 去海滩玩. Close words are 沙滩 (a sandy beach) and 海边 (the seaside in general).
column6: Wǒmen zhōumò qù hǎitān wán.
column7: We go to the beach on weekends.
column9: You go there to play or sun yourself: 去海灘玩. Close words are 沙灘 (a sandy beach) and 海邊 (the seaside in general).

column3: Land for growing crops, especially a rice paddy: 稻田, 田地, 田里. It is also a common surname. It is a picture of a field divided into four sections.
column6: Yéye zài tián lǐ gōngzuò.
column7: Grandpa works in the field.
column9: Land for growing crops, especially a rice paddy: 稻田, 田地, 田里. It is also a common surname. It is a picture of a field divided into four sections.

column3: Two main uses. For wind: 刮风, 刮大风, 刮台风 (a typhoon hits). And to scrape or shave: 刮胡子 is to shave one's beard.
column6: Jīntiān wàimiàn guā dàfēng.
column7: It is very windy outside today.
column9: Two main uses. For wind: 颳風, 颳大風, 颳颱風 (a typhoon hits). And to scrape or shave: 刮鬍子 is to shave one's beard.

column3: Used with 看, since watching the sunrise is something people plan: 看日出. It also marks time: 日出之前. The opposite is 日落. 出 is a foot stepping out of a cave; the old reading of it as a plant growing out was a mistake.
column4: 我们早上五点去看日出。
column5: 我們早上五點去看日出。
column6: Wǒmen zǎoshang wǔ diǎn qù kàn rìchū.
column7: We go to watch the sunrise at five in the morning.
column9: Used with 看, since watching the sunrise is something people plan: 看日出. It also marks time: 日出之前. The opposite is 日落. 出 is a foot stepping out of a cave; the old reading of it as a plant growing out was a mistake.

column3: Gold as a thing, in spoken Chinese: 一块金子. 黄金 is the usual word for the material or the market, and 金 alone is in compounds such as 金牌 and 金钱. 金 originally referred to copper; later it was extended to metal as a whole, and then to gold.
column6: Tā zài shān lǐ zhǎodào le jīnzi.
column7: He found gold in the mountains.
column9: Gold as a thing, in spoken Chinese: 一塊金子. 黃金 is the usual word for the material or the market, and 金 alone is in compounds such as 金牌 and 金錢. 金 originally referred to copper; later it was extended to metal as a whole, and then to gold.

column3: Mostly in compounds: 木头 (wood), 木板 (a board), 树木. It can also mean numb. It is a picture of a tree, with branches on top and roots at the bottom.
column4: 这张桌子是木头的，不是铁的。
column5: 這張桌子是木頭的，不是鐵的。
column6: Zhè zhāng zhuōzi shì mù tou de, bù shì tiě de.
column7: This table is wooden, not iron.
column9: Mostly in compounds: 木頭 (wood), 木板 (a board), 樹木. It can also mean numb. It is a picture of a tree, with branches on top and roots at the bottom.

column3: Mostly in compounds: 石头 (a stone), 宝石 (a gem), 石油 (petroleum), 石像 (a stone statue).
column6: Zhè zuò qiáo shì shí tou zuò de.
column7: This bridge is made of stone.
column9: Mostly in compounds: 石頭 (a stone), 寶石 (a gem), 石油 (petroleum), 石像 (a stone statue).

column3: Written-style; in speech people say 城市. 都市 stresses a large, busy, modern city and works as a modifier: 大都市, 都市生活, 都市人. Here 都 means a capital city or metropolis.
column6: Dūshì de shēnghuó jiézòu hěn kuài.
column7: The pace of life in the city is fast.
column9: Written-style; in speech people say 城市. 都市 stresses a large, busy, modern city and works as a modifier: 大都市, 都市生活, 都市人. Here 都 means a capital city or metropolis.

column3: The school subject or the features of a place: 地理课, 地理位置. 理 here means a pattern or principle, the same 理 as in 物理 (physics), 心理 (psychology) and 道理 (reason).
column6: Wǒ zuì xǐhuan shàng dìlǐ kè.
column7: I like geography class the most.
column9: The school subject or the features of a place: 地理課, 地理位置. 理 here means a pattern or principle, the same 理 as in 物理 (physics), 心理 (psychology) and 道理 (reason).

column3: Literally "under heaven": the whole world, or all of China in old texts. Today it lives mostly in sayings: 天下没有白吃的午餐 (there is no free lunch), 天下太平 (peace in the world).
column6: Tiānxià méiyǒu bái chī de wǔcān.
column7: There is no such thing as a free lunch.
column9: Literally "under heaven": the whole world, or all of China in old texts. Today it lives mostly in sayings: 天下沒有白吃的午餐 (there is no free lunch), 天下太平 (peace in the world).

column3: The large room in a school, company or government building for meetings and ceremonies: 大礼堂, 在礼堂开会. For a small meeting, a 会议室 is the room.
column6: Bìyè diǎnlǐ zài lǐtáng jǔxíng.
column7: The graduation ceremony is held in the auditorium.
column9: The large room in a school, company or government building for meetings and ceremonies: 大禮堂, 在禮堂開會. For a small meeting, a 會議室 is the room.

column3: Goods laid out on the ground or a cloth: 摆地摊 is to set up a stall, and 地摊货 is cheap goods from one. The stalls of a night market are 摊位, the vendors 摊贩.
column4: 他在夜市摆地摊卖衣服。
column5: 他在夜市擺地攤賣衣服。
column6: Tā zài yèshì bǎi dìtān mài yīfu.
column7: He sets up a street stall at the night market and sells clothes.
column9: Goods laid out on the ground or a cloth: 擺地攤 is to set up a stall, and 地攤貨 is cheap goods from one. The stalls of a night market are 攤位, the vendors 攤販.

column3: The place where a conference or event is held: 会场在哪里? 进入会场. For the room of a small meeting, say 会议室.
column6: Huìchǎng zài èr lóu.
column7: The venue is on the second floor.
column9: The place where a conference or event is held: 會場在哪裡? 進入會場. For the room of a small meeting, say 會議室.

column3: Mostly going out for an errand, as in 上街买菜, or taking to the streets in a protest: 上街抗议. For strolling and shopping for fun, 逛街 is the usual word.
column6: Māma shàngjiē mǎi cài le.
column7: Mom went out to buy groceries.
column9: Mostly going out for an errand, as in 上街買菜, or taking to the streets in a protest: 上街抗議. For strolling and shopping for fun, 逛街 is the usual word.

column3: A "tram" or electric train that runs on rails. In Taiwan a city's metro trains are 捷运, even when the talk is of Japan's; an electric car is 电动车. 电 "electric, lightning" is 曰 with 乚; 车 "vehicle" is a picture of a cart seen from above.
column6: Rìběn de diànchē hěn zhǔnshí.
column7: Japan's trains are very punctual.
column9: A "tram" or electric train that runs on rails. In Taiwan a city's metro trains are 捷運, even when the talk is of Japan's; an electric car is 電動車. 電 "electric, lightning" has 雨 "rain" on top, as lightning comes with storms; 車 "vehicle" is a picture of a cart seen from above.

column3: The standard word for a truck; 货车 is another common one. A big one is 大卡车, and the measure word is 辆: 一辆卡车. The 卡 is a loanword, from English "car".
column6: Yī liàng dà kǎchē tíng zài lùbiān.
column7: A big truck is parked by the roadside.
column9: The standard word for a truck; 貨車 is another common one. A big one is 大卡車, and the measure word is 輛: 一輛卡車. The 卡 is a loanword, from English "car".

column3: It names the whole set of lights, and it is how directions are given: 到红绿灯右转 "turn right at the light". For one color, say 等红灯 or 闯红灯 (run a red).
column6: Qiánmiàn yǒu yī gè hónglǜdēng.
column7: There is a traffic light up ahead.
column9: It names the whole set of lights, and it is how directions are given: 到紅綠燈右轉 "turn right at the light". For one color, say 等紅燈 or 闖紅燈 (run a red).

column3: The usual verb is 换 (换轮胎); a blowout is 爆胎, and 轮胎没气了 says it is flat. The bare 胎 can stand for the tire too, as in 爆胎.
column6: Wǒ de qìchē lúntāi méi qì le.
column7: My car's tire is flat.
column9: The usual verb is 換 (換輪胎); a blowout is 爆胎, and 輪胎沒氣了 says it is flat. The bare 胎 can stand for the tire too, as in 爆胎.

column3: A verb with its object built in, so a place cannot follow it: say 在台北迷路, not 迷路台北. It splits around 了: 迷了路 "got lost".
column6: Wǒ zài Táiběi mílù le.
column7: I got lost in Taipei.
column9: A verb with its object built in, so a place cannot follow it: say 在台北迷路, not 迷路台北. It splits around 了: 迷了路 "got lost".

column3: Two uses: making it in time for a vehicle or deadline (赶不上 "can't make it"), and catching up with others: 他很快就赶上了大家. 来得及 also says "in time".
column4: 我赶上了最后一班火车。
column5: 我趕上了最後一班火車。
column6: Wǒ gǎnshàng le zuìhòu yī bān huǒchē.
column7: I caught the last train.
column9: Two uses: making it in time for a vehicle or deadline (趕不上 "can't make it"), and catching up with others: 他很快就趕上了大家. 來得及 also says "in time".

column3: Formal: it goes before a place or a time, as in 距今三年. In speech the everyday word is 离, and the noun "distance" is 距离.
column6: Xuéxiào jù chēzhàn bù yuǎn.
column7: The school is not far from the station.
column9: Formal: it goes before a place or a time, as in 距今三年. In speech the everyday word is 离, and the noun "distance" is 距离.

column3: A particular scheduled flight, as announced or on the board: 班机延误, 下一班班机. 班机 is the everyday word in Taiwan, while the mainland mostly says 航班 and keeps 班机 for formal or news language. 机 is the aircraft in 飞机 and 直升机.
column6: Wǒmen de bānjī yánwù le.
column7: Our flight is delayed.
column9: A particular scheduled flight, as announced or on the board: 班機延誤, 下一班班機. 班機 is the everyday word in Taiwan, while the mainland mostly says 航班 and keeps 班機 for formal or news language. 機 is the aircraft in 飛機 and 直升機.

column3: Formal, for announcements, news and schedules; in speech 到 is the normal word. It takes the place directly, with no 到 before it: 抵达机场, 准时抵达.
column4: 飞机将在十点抵达台北。
column5: 飛機將在十點抵達台北。
column6: Fēijī jiāng zài shí diǎn dǐdá Táiběi.
column7: The plane will arrive in Taipei at ten o'clock.
column9: Formal, for announcements, news and schedules; in speech 到 is the normal word. It takes the place directly, with no 到 before it: 抵達機場, 準時抵達.

column3: It points back to a day just mentioned or already fixed, never to "today" (that is 今天): 活动当天 "on the day of the event", 当天来回, 当天的报纸.
column6: Wǒmen dàngtiān jiù huílái le.
column7: We came back the same day.
column9: It points back to a day just mentioned or already fixed, never to "today" (that is 今天): 活動當天 "on the day of the event", 當天來回, 當天的報紙.

column3: Doubling a time word gives "every": 天天, 年年. It usually comes with 都 before the verb (年年都去), and it appears in the New Year wish 年年有余. 年 first meant "harvest" before it came to mean "year".
column6: Tā niánnián dōu huí lǎojiā guònián.
column7: Every year he goes back to his hometown for the New Year.
column9: Doubling a time word gives "every": 天天, 年年. It usually comes with 都 before the verb (年年都去), and it appears in the New Year wish 年年有余. 年 first meant "harvest" before it came to mean "year".

column3: It goes before the verb, usually with 都: 天天都运动. 每天 means the same and is a bit more neutral. The doubling works like 年年 and 人人.
column6: Wǒ tiāntiān zǒulù shàngbān.
column7: I walk to work every day.
column9: It goes before the verb, usually with 都: 天天都運動. 每天 means the same and is a bit more neutral. The doubling works like 年年 and 人人.

column3: Never used bare: it comes with a number or a pointing word, as in 一辈子, 这辈子, 下辈子. With 都 and a negative it means "never in my whole life".
column6: Wǒ zhè bèizi dōu bù huì wàngjì.
column7: I will never forget it as long as I live.
column9: Never used bare: it comes with a number or a pointing word, as in 一輩子, 這輩子, 下輩子. With 都 and a negative it means "never in my whole life".

column3: A short, passing state: 一时想不起来, 一时冲动 "on an impulse", 一时之间. It is not a stretch you can measure; for that use 一会儿.
column4: 我一时想不起来他的名字。
column5: 我一時想不起來他的名字。
column6: Wǒ yīshí xiǎng bù qǐlái tā de míngzi.
column7: I can't recall his name for the moment.
column9: A short, passing state: 一時想不起來, 一時衝動 "on an impulse", 一時之間. It is not a stretch you can measure; for that use 一會兒.

column3: Formal, for something hoped for or planned, not for a time already fixed: 早日完成, 早日见面, and the stock wish 祝你早日康复.
column6: Zhù nǐ zǎorì kāngfù.
column7: I hope you recover soon.
column9: Formal, for something hoped for or planned, not for a time already fixed: 早日完成, 早日見面, and the stock wish 祝你早日康復.

column3: A polite way to put something off: 改天再聊, 改天见. It often just means "not today" and sets no real date.
column6: Wǒ jīntiān yǒu shì, gǎitiān zài yuē.
column7: I'm busy today, let's meet another day.
column9: A polite way to put something off: 改天再聊, 改天見. It often just means "not today" and sets no real date.

column3: A place or building of historic interest, common in 名胜古迹 and 参观古迹. For movable objects in a museum the word is 文物.
column6: Táinán yǒu hěn duō gǔjì.
column7: Tainan has many historic sites.
column9: A place or building of historic interest, common in 名勝古跡 and 參觀古蹟. For movable objects in a museum the word is 文物.

column3: The pairs 忽冷忽热 "now cold, now hot" and 忽高忽低 are common in speech. 忽 alone for "suddenly" is literary (忽见); speech uses 忽然, which also holds 忽 in 忽略.
column6: Tiānqì hū lěng hū rè.
column7: The weather is now cold, now hot.
column9: The pairs 忽冷忽熱 "now cold, now hot" and 忽高忽低 are common in speech. 忽 alone for "suddenly" is literary (忽見); speech uses 忽然, which also holds 忽 in 忽略.

column3: It goes before a number, measure and verb, for something repeated without a break: 一连三天, 一连说了三次. The same 连 is in 连续 and 连接.
column6: Tā yīlián sān tiān méi shuìjiào.
column7: He did not sleep for three days in a row.
column9: It goes before a number, measure and verb, for something repeated without a break: 一連三天, 一連說了三次. The same 連 is in 連續 and 連接.

column3: For a habit or rule: 他从不喝酒, 我从不迟到. 从来不 says the same in speech; for "have never done it" in one's experience use 从来没有.
column6: Tā cóngbù hē jiǔ.
column7: He never drinks.
column9: For a habit or rule: 他從不喝酒, 我從不遲到. 從來不 says the same in speech; for "have never done it" in one's experience use 從來沒有.

column3: A measure word for things strung or bunched together: 一串钥匙, 一串葡萄. As a verb it means "to string together": 串起来. Skewers are 肉串.
column6: Tā mǎi le yī chuàn pútáo.
column7: He bought a bunch of grapes.
column9: A measure word for things strung or bunched together: 一串鑰匙, 一串葡萄. As a verb it means "to string together": 串起來. Skewers are 肉串.

column3: The measure word for class periods and lectures: 一堂课, 上完这堂课. It also means a hall, as in 教堂 "church" and 礼堂 "auditorium".
column6: Zhè táng kè hěn yǒu yìsi.
column7: This class is very interesting.
column9: The measure word for class periods and lectures: 一堂課, 上完這堂課. It also means a hall, as in 教堂 "church" and 禮堂 "auditorium".

column3: In Taiwan the meter is 公尺 in writing and speech (一百公尺); on the mainland it is 米. Its relatives 公分, 公斤 and 公克 follow the same 公.
column4: 这栋大楼有两百公尺高。
column5: 這棟大樓有兩百公尺高。
column6: Zhè dòng dàlóu yǒu liǎng bǎi gōngchǐ gāo.
column7: This building is two hundred meters tall.
column9: In Taiwan the meter is 公尺 in writing and speech (一百公尺); on the mainland it is 米. Its relatives 公分, 公斤 and 公克 follow the same 公.

column3: In Taiwan height is given in it: 一百七十公分. The mainland usually says 一米七 and writes 厘米 for centimeter. It is not the gram, which is 公克.
column6: Tā yī bǎi bāshí gōngfēn gāo.
column7: He is 180 centimeters tall.
column9: In Taiwan height is given in it: 一百七十公分. The mainland usually says 一米七 and writes 厘米 for centimeter. It is not the gram, which is 公克.

column3: The full word for gram on a Taiwan label or recipe: 五百公克. The mainland writes 五百克. 公斤 is the kilogram.
column6: Zhè bāo táng yǒu wǔ bǎi gōngkè.
column7: This bag of sugar weighs five hundred grams.
column9: The full word for gram on a Taiwan label or recipe: 五百公克. The mainland writes 五百克. 公斤 is the kilogram.

column3: Taiwan's unit of floor area, used for buying and renting homes (三十坪的房子, with prices quoted 每坪). The mainland uses square meters, 平方米. The unit was borrowed from the Japanese one during the Japanese colonial period.
column6: Zhè jiān gōngyù yǒu sānshí píng.
column7: This apartment is thirty ping.
column9: Taiwan's unit of floor area, used for buying and renting homes (三十坪的房子, with prices quoted 每坪). The mainland uses square meters, 平方米. The unit was borrowed from the Japanese one during the Japanese colonial period.

column3: The pattern is 逼 plus a person plus a verb: 逼我做, 逼他说实话. It stresses pressure against the person's will. 逼近 means "to close in on".
column4: 不要逼我做不想做的事。
column5: 不要逼我做不想做的事。
column6: Bùyào bī wǒ zuò bù xiǎng zuò de shì.
column7: Don't force me to do things I don't want to do.
column9: The pattern is 逼 plus a person plus a verb: 逼我做, 逼他說實話. It stresses pressure against the person's will. 逼近 means "to close in on".

column3: Meeting something by chance, a person or a bit of luck: 碰上老朋友, 碰上下雨 "get caught in the rain". 碰到 means almost the same and is just as common.
column4: 我在路上碰上了老同学。
column5: 我在路上碰上了老同學。
column6: Wǒ zài lùshang pèngshàng le lǎo tóngxué.
column7: I ran into an old classmate on the way.
column9: Meeting something by chance, a person or a bit of luck: 碰上老朋友, 碰上下雨 "get caught in the rain". 碰到 means almost the same and is just as common.

column3: A verb with its object: 省了不少钱 "saved quite a lot". It also works as an adjective, "economical": 这个方法很省钱.
column6: Zìjǐ zuòfàn bǐjiào shěngqián.
column7: Cooking for yourself saves more money.
column9: A verb with its object: 省了不少錢 "saved quite a lot". It also works as an adjective, "economical": 這個方法很省錢.

column3: What the cashier does: 找您五十元 "here is 50 yuan change", and 不用找钱了 "keep the change". 找零 is the other everyday way to say it.
column6: Bùyòng zhǎoqián le.
column7: Keep the change.
column9: What the cashier does: 找您五十元 "here is 50 yuan change", and 不用找錢了 "keep the change". 找零 is the other everyday way to say it.

column3: Haggling at markets and small shops; 可以讲价吗？ is the stock question. Taiwan also says 杀价 for it, the mainland 砍价 (and 还价). 不二价 means a fixed price.
column6: Zài yèshì kěyǐ jiǎngjià.
column7: You can bargain at the night market.
column9: Haggling at markets and small shops; 可以講價嗎？ is the stock question. Taiwan also says 殺價 for it, the mainland 砍價 (and 還價). 不二價 means a fixed price.

column3: The sign over a shop door, and by extension the shop's good name: 砸招牌 "ruin its reputation". 招牌菜 is a restaurant's signature dish.
column6: Zhè jiā diàn de zhāopai hěn dà.
column7: This shop's sign is very big.
column9: The sign over a shop door, and by extension the shop's good name: 砸招牌 "ruin its reputation". 招牌菜 is a restaurant's signature dish.

column3: The poster for a film, concert or event: 电影海报, 贴海报. Its measure word is 张: 一张海报.
column4: 墙上贴着一张电影海报。
column5: 牆上貼著一張電影海報。
column6: Qiáng shàng tiēzhe yī zhāng diànyǐng hǎibào.
column7: There is a movie poster on the wall.
column9: The poster for a film, concert or event: 電影海報, 貼海報. Its measure word is 張: 一張海報.

column3: The kind of use comes first: 日常用品, 办公用品, 运动用品. It names a whole group of goods, so a single item is called by its own name.
column6: Zhè jiā diàn mài rìcháng yòngpǐn.
column7: This shop sells daily necessities.
column9: The kind of use comes first: 日常用品, 辦公用品, 運動用品. It names a whole group of goods, so a single item is called by its own name.

column3: Being taken in by a trick or a false ad. The victim is the subject, and the trickster can come inside: 上了他的当. 小心别上当 is the warning.
column4: 我上当了，这个东西是假的。
column5: 我上當了，這個東西是假的。
column6: Wǒ shàngdàng le, zhège dōngxi shì jiǎ de.
column7: I was fooled, this thing is fake.
column9: Being taken in by a trick or a false ad. The victim is the subject, and the trickster can come inside: 上了他的當. 小心別上當 is the warning.

column3: Usually followed by 都: 人人都知道. It also opens sayings such as 人人有责 "everyone has a duty". The doubling is the same as in 天天 and 年年.
column6: Rénrén dōu xǐhuan tā.
column7: Everyone likes him.
column9: Usually followed by 都: 人人都知道. It also opens sayings such as 人人有責 "everyone has a duty". The doubling is the same as in 天天 and 年年.

column3: A spoken adverb before the verb, for a small but real amount: 多多少少知道一些. It is not the question word 多少 "how many".
column6: Tā duōduōshǎoshǎo zhīdào yīxiē.
column7: He knows something about it, more or less.
column9: A spoken adverb before the verb, for a small but real amount: 多多少少知道一些. It is not the question word 多少 "how many".

column3: Every kind, followed by 都 right away: 样样都好, 样样都会. In writing it can be followed by 俱, as in 样样俱全.
column6: Tā yàngyàng dōu huì.
column7: She can do everything.
column9: Every kind, followed by 都 right away: 樣樣都好, 樣樣都會. In writing it can be followed by 俱, as in 樣樣俱全.

column3: It sits before a noun and takes 的: 各式各样的人, 各式各样的商品. 各种各样 means the same.
column4: 夜市里有各式各样的小吃。
column5: 夜市裡有各式各樣的小吃。
column6: Yèshì lǐ yǒu gèshìgèyàng de xiǎochī.
column7: There are all kinds of snacks at the night market.
column9: It sits before a noun and takes 的: 各式各樣的人, 各式各樣的商品. 各種各樣 means the same.

column3: It sets an upper limit and goes before the number: 最多十个, 最多只能. The opposite is 最少 "at least". As "the most" it appears in 最多人.
column6: Wǒ zuìduō zhǐ néng děng shí fēnzhōng.
column7: I can wait ten minutes at most.
column9: It sets an upper limit and goes before the number: 最多十個, 最多只能. The opposite is 最少 "at least". As "the most" it appears in 最多人.

column3: Only for the other person: you answer 我姓王, never 我贵姓王. 免贵姓王 is the modest reply, which turns the honor down.
column6: Qǐngwèn nín guìxìng?
column7: May I ask your surname?
column9: Only for the other person: you answer 我姓王, never 我貴姓王. 免貴姓王 is the modest reply, which turns the honor down.

column3: It takes 向 or 替 for the person: 向你的家人问好, 替我向他问好. To greet someone face to face you say 你好 instead.
column6: Qǐng tì wǒ xiàng nǐ fùmǔ wènhǎo.
column7: Please give my regards to your parents.
column9: It takes 向 or 替 for the person: 向你的家人問好, 替我向他問好. To greet someone face to face you say 你好 instead.

column3: A formal, real apology: 向他道歉, 道歉信. It splits around its object like a verb phrase (道了歉); for a light "sorry" use 对不起.
column6: Nǐ yīnggāi xiàng tā dàoqiàn.
column7: You should apologize to him.
column9: A formal, real apology: 向他道歉, 道歉信. It splits around its object like a verb phrase (道了歉); for a light "sorry" use 對不起.

column3: Mostly doubled or in compounds: 谢谢, 多谢, 感谢. On its own it is the reply 不用谢 "don't mention it". 谢绝 is to decline politely.
column4: 不用谢，这是我应该做的。
column5: 不用謝，這是我應該做的。
column6: Bù yòng xiè, zhè shì wǒ yīnggāi zuò de.
column7: Don't mention it, it is what I should do.
column9: Mostly doubled or in compounds: 謝謝, 多謝, 感謝. On its own it is the reply 不用謝 "don't mention it". 謝絕 is to decline politely.

column3: The person is the object and the fault follows: 原谅我迟到, 原谅他. 请原谅我 is the standard way to ask for forgiveness.
column6: Qǐng yuánliàng wǒ chídào.
column7: Please forgive me for being late.
column9: The person is the object and the fault follows: 原諒我遲到, 原諒他. 請原諒我 is the standard way to ask for forgiveness.

column3: For a place, face or thing you do not know: 陌生人 "stranger", 对这里很陌生. The opposite is 熟悉. 陌 appears only together with 生.
column6: Wǒ duì zhège chéngshì hěn mòshēng.
column7: I am not familiar with this city.
column9: For a place, face or thing you do not know: 陌生人 "stranger", 對這裡很陌生. The opposite is 熟悉. 陌 appears only together with 生.

column3: Describes someone who senses what others need: 他很体贴, 体贴的先生. It can also be a verb with an object: 体贴别人.
column6: Tā duì jiārén hěn tǐtiē.
column7: He is very considerate toward his family.
column9: Describes someone who senses what others need: 他很體貼, 體貼的先生. It can also be a verb with an object: 體貼別人.

column3: For a person or a voice: 温柔的声音, 个性温柔. It is said most often of women, though a man can be 温柔 too.
column6: Tā de shēngyīn hěn wēnróu.
column7: Her voice is very gentle.
column9: For a person or a voice: 溫柔的聲音, 個性溫柔. It is said most often of women, though a man can be 溫柔 too.

column3: A school word for spoken practice in a language: 英语会话, 会话课, 基本会话. For an ordinary chat use 聊天 or 谈话.
column4: 我每周上两堂中文会话课。
column5: 我每週上兩堂中文會話課。
column6: Wǒ měi zhōu shàng liǎng táng Zhōngwén huìhuà kè.
column7: I have two Chinese conversation classes a week.
column9: A school word for spoken practice in a language: 英語會話, 會話課, 基本會話. For an ordinary chat use 聊天 or 談話.

column3: In Taiwan 连络 and 联络 are used interchangeably; on the mainland 联络 is the usual form and 联系 is more common in speech. Typical uses: 保持连络, 连络电话.
column6: Wǒmen bǎochí liánluò ba.
column7: Let's stay in touch.
column9: In Taiwan 連絡 and 聯絡 are used interchangeably; on the mainland 聯絡 is the usual form and 聯繫 is more common in speech. Typical uses: 保持連絡, 連絡電話.

column3: A spoken word with a note of disbelief: 太夸张了 "that's over the top", 说得很夸张. It also describes anything extreme, such as 价格很夸张.
column6: Nǐ shuō de tài kuāzhāng le.
column7: You are exaggerating too much.
column9: A spoken word with a note of disbelief: 太誇張了 "that's over the top", 說得很誇張. It also describes anything extreme, such as 價格很誇張.

column3: Praise for children and pets that do as told: 这孩子很乖, 乖乖听话 "be good and listen". Adults also say 乖 warmly to a child.
column6: Zhège háizi hěn guāi.
column7: This child is very well-behaved.
column9: Praise for children and pets that do as told: 這孩子很乖, 乖乖聽話 "be good and listen". Adults also say 乖 warmly to a child.

column3: A compliment for a child or young person who sees what others need and acts older than their age. The opposite, 不懂事, is a mild reproach: 别这么不懂事.
column4: 她虽然年纪小，但很懂事。
column5: 她雖然年紀小，但很懂事。
column6: Tā suīrán niánjì xiǎo, dàn hěn dǒngshì.
column7: Although she is young, she is very sensible.
column9: A compliment for a child or young person who sees what others need and acts older than their age. The opposite, 不懂事, is a mild reproach: 別這麼不懂事.

column3: It describes a person (他很谦虚) and also how they speak: 谦虚地说. The modest reply to praise is 哪里哪里 or 不敢当. The opposite is 骄傲, and 谦虚使人进步 is a well-known saying.
column4: 他很有才华，但是很谦虚。
column5: 他很有才華，但是很謙虛。
column6: Tā hěn yǒu cáihuá, dànshì hěn qiānxū.
column7: He is very talented, but also modest.
column9: It describes a person (他很謙虛) and also how they speak: 謙虛地說. The modest reply to praise is 哪裡哪裡 or 不敢當. The opposite is 驕傲, and 謙虛使人進步 is a well-known saying.

column3: It describes a lasting nature, not today's mood: 个性开朗, 开朗的人. The opposite is 忧郁, gloomy, or 内向, reserved.
column6: Tā de gèxìng hěn kāilǎng.
column7: She has a cheerful personality.
column9: It describes a lasting nature, not today's mood: 個性開朗, 開朗的人. The opposite is 憂鬱, gloomy, or 內向, reserved.

column3: It takes the parents as its object (孝顺父母) or describes a child: 孝顺的孩子. It names a real virtue and is said with respect.
column6: Tā hěn xiàoshùn fùmǔ.
column7: He is very good to his parents.
column9: It takes the parents as its object (孝順父母) or describes a child: 孝順的孩子. It names a real virtue and is said with respect.

column3: It describes a person who notices details: 她很细心, 做事细心. It can also describe how something is done: 细心照顾. The opposite is 粗心, careless.
column6: Tā zuòshì hěn xìxīn.
column7: She is very careful in her work.
column9: It describes a person who notices details: 她很細心, 做事細心. It can also describe how something is done: 細心照顧. The opposite is 粗心, careless.

column3: Two senses, and the context decides: proud of someone or something, in a good way (我为你感到骄傲, 以…为骄傲), or arrogant, in a bad way (他太骄傲了).
column6: Wǒ wèi nǐ gǎndào jiāo'ào.
column7: I feel proud of you.
column9: Two senses, and the context decides: proud of someone or something, in a good way (我為你感到驕傲, 以…為驕傲), or arrogant, in a bad way (他太驕傲了).

column3: It describes a mind that is unclear, not just a lack of knowledge: 老糊涂了 for confusion with age, 一时糊涂 for a moment of confusion, and 装糊涂 for pretending not to understand.
column6: Tā niánjì dà le, yǒudiǎn hútu.
column7: He is old now and a little muddled.
column9: It describes a mind that is unclear, not just a lack of knowledge: 老糊塗了 for confusion with age, 一時糊塗 for a moment of confusion, and 裝糊塗 for pretending not to understand.

column3: About holding back a feeling or pain, often asked of someone: 请你忍耐一下, or 忍耐不住 when it is too much. 忍受 takes the unpleasant thing itself: 忍受痛苦. The bound 耐 also builds 耐心 and 耐用.
column6: Qǐng nǐ zài rěnnài yīxià.
column7: Please bear with it a little longer.
column9: About holding back a feeling or pain, often asked of someone: 請你忍耐一下, or 忍耐不住 when it is too much. 忍受 takes the unpleasant thing itself: 忍受痛苦. The bound 耐 also builds 耐心 and 耐用.

column3: It names one's strong point, above all a skill like cooking: 很拿手, 对做菜很拿手. Two set phrases: 拿手菜, a signature dish, and 拿手好戏, the thing one does best.
column6: Shuōdào zuòcài, wǒ zuì náshǒu.
column7: When it comes to cooking, I am best at it.
column9: It names one's strong point, above all a skill like cooking: 很拿手, 對做菜很拿手. Two set phrases: 拿手菜, a signature dish, and 拿手好戲, the thing one does best.

column3: Fierce, vicious: 那只狗很凶 "that dog is fierce", 凶手 "murderer", 凶恶 "ferocious". It is also said of a person scolding, 她骂得很凶. For animals, 凶猛 is "fierce": 凶猛的老虎 "a fierce tiger".
column6: Nà zhī gǒu hěn xiōng.
column7: That dog is fierce.
column9: Fierce, vicious: 那隻狗很兇 "that dog is fierce", 兇手 "murderer", 兇惡 "ferocious". It is also said of a person scolding, 她罵得很兇. For animals, 兇猛 is "fierce": 兇猛的老虎 "a fierce tiger".

column3: A little formal, and common in wishes and greetings: 祝你周末愉快, 旅途愉快. It also describes a mood or an experience: 心情愉快, 愉快的一天.
column6: Zhù nǐ zhōumò yúkuài!
column7: Have a nice weekend!
column9: A little formal, and common in wishes and greetings: 祝你周末愉快, 旅途愉快. It also describes a mood or an experience: 心情愉快, 愉快的一天.

column3: It is about feeling relaxed, without tension: 一个人很自在, 自由自在. 不自在 means ill at ease, for example around a stranger.
column6: Yī ge rén zhù hěn zìzai.
column7: Living alone is very comfortable.
column9: It is about feeling relaxed, without tension: 一個人很自在, 自由自在. 不自在 means ill at ease, for example around a stranger.

column3: A verb for putting one's own mind at rest: 请安心 means do not worry, 安心工作 means work without distraction, 让人安心 puts others at ease, and 我安心了 means I can relax now.
column4: 听到你平安，我就安心了。
column5: 聽到你平安，我就安心了。
column6: Tīngdào nǐ píng'ān, wǒ jiù ānxīn le.
column7: When I heard you were safe, I felt at ease.
column9: A verb for putting one's own mind at rest: 請安心 means do not worry, 安心工作 means work without distraction, 讓人安心 puts others at ease, and 我安心了 means I can relax now.

column3: It describes a life or a society: 生活安定, 社会安定. As a verb: 安定下来, settle down. 稳定 is close, and also covers jobs, moods, prices and the economy.
column6: Tā xiànzài de shēnghuó hěn āndìng.
column7: His life is settled now.
column9: It describes a life or a society: 生活安定, 社會安定. As a verb: 安定下來, settle down. 穩定 is close, and also covers jobs, moods, prices and the economy.

column3: Both a noun and a verb: 有很多烦恼, 别烦恼了, 烦恼的事. It is mental trouble, more a feeling than a problem with a plan.
column6: Tā zuìjìn yǒu hěn duō fánnǎo.
column7: He has many worries recently.
column9: Both a noun and a verb: 有很多煩惱, 別煩惱了, 煩惱的事. It is mental trouble, more a feeling than a problem with a plan.

column3: A strong wish for something not possible or not happening yet, followed by the wished action: 恨不得马上回家, 我恨不得飞过去. It does not mean hate.
column6: Wǒ hènbude mǎshàng huíjiā.
column7: I can't wait to go home right now.
column9: A strong wish for something not possible or not happening yet, followed by the wished action: 恨不得馬上回家, 我恨不得飛過去. It does not mean hate.

column3: An angry reaction to someone's behavior: 真可恶, 可恶的小偷. On its own, 可恶！ is like saying damn it. Here 恶 is read wù, to hate, not è, evil.
column6: Zhège xiǎotōu zhēn kěwù!
column7: This thief is really hateful!
column9: An angry reaction to someone's behavior: 真可惡, 可惡的小偷. On its own, 可惡！ is like saying damn it. Here 惡 is read wù, to hate, not è, evil.

column3: The 了 and the person go inside it: 吓了一跳, 吓我一跳. It is used for a pleasant or neutral surprise as well as for fear.
column4: 她突然大叫，把我吓一跳。
column5: 她突然大叫，把我嚇一跳。
column6: Tā tūrán dàjiào, bǎ wǒ xiàyītiào.
column7: She suddenly yelled and startled me.
column9: The 了 and the person go inside it: 嚇了一跳, 嚇我一跳. It is used for a pleasant or neutral surprise as well as for fear.

column3: A slightly formal word for surprise at something unexpected: 很惊讶, 感到惊讶, 令人惊讶. It carries no fear, unlike 害怕.
column6: Dàjiā dōu hěn jīngyà.
column7: Everyone is surprised.
column9: A slightly formal word for surprise at something unexpected: 很驚訝, 感到驚訝, 令人驚訝. It carries no fear, unlike 害怕.

column3: A verb plus object, so 了 and a quantity go between: 发了一顿脾气. The target takes 对 or 向: 对孩子发脾气. 脾气 alone means temper: 好脾气, 坏脾气.
column6: Tā chángcháng duì háizi fāpíqì.
column7: He often loses his temper with the children.
column9: A verb plus object, so 了 and a quantity go between: 發了一頓脾氣. The target takes 對 or 向: 對孩子發脾氣. 脾氣 alone means temper: 好脾氣, 壞脾氣.

column3: It is about people's attitude, not the weather, which is just 冷: 态度冷淡, 反应冷淡. Business can also be slack: 生意冷淡.
column6: Tā duì wǒ de tàidù hěn lěngdàn.
column7: His attitude toward me is very cold.
column9: It is about people's attitude, not the weather, which is just 冷: 態度冷淡, 反應冷淡. Business can also be slack: 生意冷淡.

column3: It names the difficulty or failure itself: 遇到挫折, 面对挫折, and 挫折感 for the feeling of frustration. The older form of 折 showed an axe cutting a tree in half.
column6: Tā yùdào cuòzhé yě bù fàngqì.
column7: Even when he meets setbacks, he does not give up.
column9: It names the difficulty or failure itself: 遇到挫折, 面對挫折, and 挫折感 for the feeling of frustration. The older form of 折 showed an axe cutting a tree in half.

column3: Spoken. It starts a clause and gives the bad result of what was just said (快一点，要不然会迟到), or offers an alternative: 要不然我们打车吧. The shorter 不然 means the same.
column6: Kuài yīdiǎn, yàobùrán huì chídào.
column7: Hurry up, or you'll be late.
column9: Spoken. It starts a clause and gives the bad result of what was just said (快一點，要不然會遲到), or offers an alternative: 要不然我們打車吧. The shorter 不然 means the same.

column3: It opens a sentence about something that did not happen. A person or a fact follows, and the result clause often has 早就 or 就: 要不是你帮忙，我早就放弃了.
column4: 要不是你帮忙，我不可能完成。
column5: 要不是你幫忙，我不可能完成。
column6: Yàobushì nǐ bāngmáng, wǒ bù kěnéng wánchéng.
column7: If it were not for your help, I could not have finished.
column9: It opens a sentence about something that did not happen. A person or a fact follows, and the result clause often has 早就 or 就: 要不是你幫忙，我早就放棄了.

column3: It starts the second clause, after a comma, and adds a reason stronger than the first. 又 or 也 often follows it: 这家店很远，况且今天又下雨.
column4: 这家店很远，况且今天又在下雨。
column5: 這家店很遠，況且今天又在下雨。
column6: Zhè jiā diàn hěn yuǎn, kuàngqiě jīntiān yòu zài xiàyǔ.
column7: This shop is far, and besides, it is raining again today.
column9: It starts the second clause, after a comma, and adds a reason stronger than the first. 又 or 也 often follows it: 這家店很遠，況且今天又下雨.

column3: Longing with hope and some impatience: 盼望你来, 盼望已久 for long awaited, 盼望着暑假. It is stronger and more emotional than 希望.
column6: Wǒ pànwàng zhe shǔjià kuài diǎn dào.
column7: I am looking forward to the summer vacation arriving soon.
column9: Longing with hope and some impatience: 盼望你來, 盼望已久 for long awaited, 盼望著暑假. It is stronger and more emotional than 希望.

column3: It is about attention given to something, mostly in the negative: 我不在意, 别太在意. In the positive, 很在意别人的看法 means caring a lot about what others think.
column6: Biérén zěnme shuō, wǒ bù zàiyì.
column7: I don't care what others say.
column9: It is about attention given to something, mostly in the negative: 我不在意, 別太在意. In the positive, 很在意別人的看法 means caring a lot about what others think.

column3: A verb plus object: 去滑雪, with 滑雪场 for the resort and 滑雪板 for the ski or snowboard. 滑 also gives 滑冰, ice skating, and 滑板, a skateboard.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng qù Rìběn huáxuě.
column7: I want to go skiing in Japan.
column9: A verb plus object: 去滑雪, with 滑雪場 for the resort and 滑雪板 for the ski or snowboard. 滑 also gives 滑冰, ice skating, and 滑板, a skateboard.

column3: A ball game as an event. The sport comes first: 篮球赛, 棒球赛, and the usual verb is 看: 看球赛. 比赛 is the general word for a competition.
column6: Zuótiān de qiúsài hěn jīngcǎi.
column7: Yesterday's game was very exciting.
column9: A ball game as an event. The sport comes first: 籃球賽, 棒球賽, and the usual verb is 看: 看球賽. 比賽 is the general word for a competition.

column3: A player on a team: 这位球员, 职业球员. 员 marks a person with a role, as in 职员 and 演员, and 运动员 is the general word for an athlete.
column6: Zhè wèi qiúyuán pǎo de hěn kuài.
column7: This player runs very fast.
column9: A player on a team: 這位球員, 職業球員. 員 marks a person with a role, as in 職員 and 演員, and 運動員 is the general word for an athlete.

column3: It takes the person or pet being amused as its object: 逗孩子笑, 逗猫. In speech 很逗 means very funny, and 逗号 is the comma.
column6: Tā hěn huì dòu háizi xiào.
column7: He is good at making children laugh.
column9: It takes the person or pet being amused as its object: 逗孩子笑, 逗貓. In speech 很逗 means very funny, and 逗號 is the comma.

column3: Camping in the open: 去露营, 露营区 for the campsite, 露营车 for a camper or RV. Here 露 is read lù, as in outdoors; read lòu it means to show or reveal.
column6: Zhōumò wǒmen qù shān shàng lùyíng.
column7: On the weekend we go camping in the mountains.
column9: Camping in the open: 去露營, 露營區 for the campsite, 露營車 for a camper or RV. Here 露 is read lù, as in outdoors; read lòu it means to show or reveal.

column3: The plot of a film, a play or a TV drama: 剧情很精彩, 剧情简介 for the synopsis. As a genre, 剧情片 is a drama film.
column4: 这部电影的剧情很感人。
column5: 這部電影的劇情很感人。
column6: Zhè bù diànyǐng de jùqíng hěn gǎnrén.
column7: The plot of this film is very moving.
column9: The plot of a film, a play or a TV drama: 劇情很精彩, 劇情簡介 for the synopsis. As a genre, 劇情片 is a drama film.

column3: It stresses how things turn out in the end: 好的结局, 快乐的结局, 悲惨的结局, and 结局如何 for how does it end. It suits stories as well as events.
column4: 这个故事的结局很意外。
column5: 這個故事的結局很意外。
column6: Zhège gùshi de jiéjú hěn yìwài.
column7: The ending of this story is unexpected.
column9: It stresses how things turn out in the end: 好的結局, 快樂的結局, 悲慘的結局, and 結局如何 for how does it end. It suits stories as well as events.

column3: A famous singer. 歌手 is the usual word for any singer, and 歌星 stresses fame. 星 names a famous person in a field: 球星, 影星.
column6: Tā shì yī wèi yǒumíng de gēxīng.
column7: She is a famous singer.
column9: A famous singer. 歌手 is the usual word for any singer, and 歌星 stresses fame. 星 names a famous person in a field: 球星, 影星.

column3: Both a verb and a noun: 合唱一首歌, 男女合唱, 合唱团 for a choir. 合 adds togetherness, as in 合作 and 合影.
column4: 他们一起合唱了一首歌。
column5: 他們一起合唱了一首歌。
column6: Tāmen yīqǐ héchàng le yī shǒu gē.
column7: They sang a song together.
column9: Both a verb and a noun: 合唱一首歌, 男女合唱, 合唱團 for a choir. 合 adds togetherness, as in 合作 and 合影.

column3: It names an orchestra anywhere: 管弦乐团, 国家乐团. For a pop or rock band, Taiwan says 乐团, and the mainland more often 乐队. Here 乐 is music, yuè; as happy or cheerful it is lè.
column4: 这个乐团下个月来台湾表演。
column5: 這個樂團下個月來台灣表演。
column6: Zhège yuètuán xià ge yuè lái Táiwān biǎoyǎn.
column7: This band is coming to Taiwan to perform next month.
column9: It names an orchestra anywhere: 管弦樂團, 國家樂團. For a pop or rock band, Taiwan says 樂團, and the mainland more often 樂隊. Here 樂 is music, yuè; as happy or cheerful it is lè.

column3: The pitch pattern of a Chinese syllable: 四个声调, 声调错了, 练习声调. It can also mean the tone of someone's voice. For intonation across a sentence, say 语调.
column6: Zhōngwén yǒu sì ge shēngdiào.
column7: Chinese has four tones.
column9: The pitch pattern of a Chinese syllable: 四個聲調, 聲調錯了, 練習聲調. It can also mean the tone of someone's voice. For intonation across a sentence, say 語調.

column3: Unwanted loud sound, something that can be measured: 噪音太大, 噪音污染, 制造噪音. For a person or place that is noisy, the verb is 吵. It is also static in a signal.
column6: Wàimiàn de zàoyīn tài dà le.
column7: The noise outside is too loud.
column9: Unwanted loud sound, something that can be measured: 噪音太大, 噪音污染, 制造噪音. For a person or place that is noisy, the verb is 吵. It is also static in a signal.

column3: The equipment: 一套音响, 蓝牙音响 for a Bluetooth speaker. It can also mean acoustics or sound quality: 音响效果.
column6: Tā mǎi le yī tào xīn yīnxiǎng.
column7: He bought a new stereo system.
column9: The equipment: 一套音響, 藍牙音響 for a Bluetooth speaker. It can also mean acoustics or sound quality: 音響效果.

column3: 起来 after a verb of perceiving gives a first impression: 听起来不错, 听起来很有趣, or with 像: 听起来像日文. 看起来 and 闻起来 have the same shape for looks and smell.
column6: Zhège zhǔyi tīngqilai bùcuò.
column7: This idea sounds good.
column9: 起來 after a verb of perceiving gives a first impression: 聽起來不錯, 聽起來很有趣, or with 像: 聽起來像日文. 看起來 and 聞起來 have the same shape for looks and smell.

column3: Mostly a bound form: 播放 to play, 广播 to broadcast, 播报 to report on air, 播种 to sow seeds. A show can also take 播 alone: 几点播?
column6: Zhè bù jù shénme shíhou bō?
column7: When does this series air?
column9: Mostly a bound form: 播放 to play, 廣播 to broadcast, 播報 to report on air, 播種 to sow seeds. A show can also take 播 alone: 幾點播?

column3: A message left for someone who is not there: 请留言, 语音留言 for voicemail, 留言板 for a message board. Online it is also a comment under a post.
column6: Nǐ kěyǐ zài wǎngzhàn shàng liúyán.
column7: You can leave a message on the website.
